I was talking with someone at LVNAQ, and we were disucssing how annoying
the seating selection mechanic for the final table was. Specifically
because it was totally different from any other regular game of VTES. And
because seating has so much influence on the game, shouldn't it be like
every other table?

So my suggestion would be:

Seat everyone randomly. 1st seed gets to pick when they get to go in play
order (1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 5th). Play.

Comments?

Frederick Scott wrote:
> And why shouldn't it be different?

And why should it not be the same? This is, after all, a V:tES
tournament.

> The finals is
> irreparably different than preliminary round games (for instance, in that
> game wins lose their special meaning).

This is entirely a function of the rewards system. It has no bearing
on whether some players should be handicapped in favor of others.

For instance, if one were to grant a substantial "table prize" to the
game winner of the final table, or if one were to not declare a
tournament winner unless there were a winner in the final game, it
would increase the odds that all players would play to win in that
final game.

In any event, the fact that players often fail to "play to win" in the
finals has been (rightly IMHO) regarded as a problem. It was most
recently addressed by changing the tournament rules by having all
runners-up in the finals tie for second place. This, together with
the occasional preference for longer time limits in the final rounds,
helps ensure that, at least for all players BUT the top seeded player,
there will be a game-win or bust mentality.

But this reminds me that top-seeded players already walk into the
final game with a substantial advantage. They are, under current
rules, in a position to tie the final game with a lower-ranked
opponent, and still be declared a tournament winner. Why should they
be granted additionally benefits?

> Do lots of people actually think this brief, little two-and-a-half-minute
> interaction is annoying?

Well. You can add me to the list.

Messages.Author: Aaron Clark
Messages.Body:
I agree that this system is a little strange. Any CCG environment is
an inherently unfair: some players have more and/or better cards than
other players for a variety of reasons, with disposable income and
date of entry into the game being the principal ones.

In choosing final seating, the players with the most metagame
knowledge of other players' decks have an advantage. I recently got
to pick my seating at a storyline final game. I chose my predator not
because I had played against him in the tournament, but because I knew
his deck from our playgroup and someone had said, "Win Henry is
playing his Arika deck." I got about 5 minutes away from winning that
game, so I'm saying that out-of-play knowledge helped me. I had no
knowledge of two other decks at the table other than who was playing
them.

VTES rewards out-of-play factors in several ways, and this is one of
them. Maybe it should be more concretely discussed. Some people
(myself included) have qualms against scouting. Maybe we should all
be saying: "At tournaments, make sure you find out what everyone else
is playing. You must scout." That way everyone is on a similar
playing field - you didn't scout and chose the wrong seating? Well,
we told you to!

The norm, per standard rules, is that deck information is private and
remains private until revealed during play. The option of switching
decks between games helps enforce this.

decks throughout the various rounds. But there seems no reason, in
keeping with the spirit or the standard game, that we should go out of
our way to encourage players to take advantage of this fact.

to play, random seating is customary. "Any method the players
choose", while a bit vague, presumably gives a player a right to
insist on random seating where he suspects other players have
knowledge of the contents of his deck, randomness being the normal
solution to such disagreements.

Because the assumption is that you cannot prevent players from knowing
the contents of each other's decks - and also, that trying to do so
will have them not want to actually play in that tournament. So the
assumption is that everybody should be able to freely scout each
other's stuff and that they will do so to where everybody is on even
footing.

For instance: I play casually with a group of players on a weekly
basis. Those players, by virtue of their being my playgroup are at
almost every tournament I play at. Unless those players bring brand-
new, unplayed decks to a tournament I play at, I can generally
identify what their deck is within the first couple of turns. If not
by their first discard. And that's an advantage over a player that's
come in from another town for the tournament, unless I find a way to
lobotomize myself (further, har har.)

Also: Players talk between rounds. Constantly. Even if you enforce a
"you must leave the room as soon as you are done" rule - which, by the
way has been done in some groups in the past and still didn't fix this
'problem - you have to find some way to prohibit, monitor and enforce
not letting anyone answer questions like "so, how did your round go?"

Which means (assuming you believe that people will work in networks,
etc, which you clearly do believe) that you have to somehow prevent
people from ever being in a position to talk to one another privately.

So here's one possible solution: Everyone has to leave between rounds,
and go sit in a second room where a judge will be seated to make sure
nobody talks or passes notes about what they saw in a previous round.
Oh, and no two people can go to the bathroom at the same time, because
then they could inform each other.

Does that sound like a tournament you want to spend six to eight hours
at? A tournament that you are supposedly playing because it is
enjoyable and fun?

And that extreme method _still_ isn't 'fair'. Because the people whose
games are in the center of the room have a greater opportunity than
those at the edges to overhear what is being said at the neighboring
tables - and if I hear Rehlow at the neighboring table say "My War
Ghoul rushes you" (for instance) I now have his deck scouted as much
as I need to.

So now it's unfair because I overheard a bunch of people while they
played and you didn't because you were off in a corner. How are you
going to prevent me from scouting by virtue of the fact that I have
pretty sharp hearing?

Oh, whoops - got a phone call. By which I mean a text message from my
buddy telling me what he faced at his table. Going to ban cell phones
too?

And if you're not going to work to prevent people from scouting and
talking etc, then people certainly will discuss things, and the
assumption is that nobody is severely disadvantaged unless they choose
to be - everyone can, if they're going to be in the finals, ask around
beforehand to find out what decks they're facing.

Note also that scouting only benefits the players in 1st - 3rd as far
as seating goes; the fourth and fifth place finishers don't benefit
from information since they don't pick their seats.

-John Flournoy

That depends on how you measure things: "How you fare against three
rounds of randomly-determined opponents" is to me often a better
measure than "how you performed directly against the other person's
deck" - this is especially true in a game where Deck A trumps Deck B
which trumps Deck C which trumps Deck A....

Being 'better' than another deck is not always a function of 'can
directly beat it in a single game'.

Here's another counter-example: We both play identical weenie-presence
bleed decks with no bounce and no intercept. Identical to the last
card. The other three decks in the final are weenie auspex walls.

If you sit as my predator, you're going to crush me nine times out of
ten; I have no defense against your deck and my deck has the worst
possible opponent sitting as my prey.

How, exactly, does that make your deck "better" than mine? How is that
"measuring against each other?"

One game is too small a sample size to determine which deck is
"better". That's one big reason why VTES uses a multi-round format and
not an elimination-bracket format for its tournaments.

> I say give them an even playing field and let the best man win.
> That's what I call rewarding "merit".

And I will say: There's no such thing as an 'even playing field' in a
single game of VTES; your preferred method is still one that randomly
rewards a player (by virtue of 'did you happen to randomly get seated
in a favorable position for this one game or a terrible one'.)

The current system, at least, rewards a player whose deck has
performed better over the long term by allowing him to better take
advantage of freely-available information, as opposed to a crapshoot
of whether or not you sit next to a deck that trumps yours no matter
how your deck has done against a wide range of opponents in the past.

I think Robert addressed the rationale behind the seating rules for
final rounds.

My only problem with the rule is that sometimes people are forced to
make decisions with NO KNOWLEDGE of some or all of the other decks in
question. On the other hand, others have a lot of knowledge, gained
either through game play, "scouting", or out-of-tournament
experience.

This suggests an uneven playing field, that some people, including
myself, are uncomfortable with.

Maybe a simple answer to the ethics of scouting is to have all
finalists go to the table at once, introduce themselves, and give a
short description of their decks, something like in the Ralf Lammert's
tournament reports on extrala.blogspot.

Example:
1. Mark Loughman -- Tremere antitribu G4/5 Wall
2. Brandon Haas -- Dom/For Tap&Bleed
2. Preston Poulter -- Akunanse Wall
2. Robyn Tatu -- Toreador antitribu Bleed w/ Palla Grande
2. Ian Lee -- City Gangrel Dominate S&B

I'm not saying the descriptions can't be deceptive. Of course, if all
the finalists are standing there, someone might call somebody else out
for being innacurate.

The thing is, it is very hard to effectively choose your seating if
you have NO IDEA what one or more other decks do. It also doesn't
help when you don't even know what a finalist looks like. Maybe you
know the finalist's deck through scouting, but you didn't learn their
name and they aren't at the table when you have to choose your
seating. I think that happens. It is also not always possible to
scout the other finalists' decks, for any number of reasons.

With my idea, people who scout would still have an advantage. But at
least no one would be at a COMPLETE disadvantage when given the
opportunity to choose seating.

rounds. There are reasons why it is illogical to regard preliminary
standings as a reliable indicator of the best player. A mediocre

The idea that more than that is needed seems contrary to the purpose
of a final round. If it were really true that the #1 player in
preliminary standings were most deserving, we could declare him the
tournament winner and call it a day.

But obviously it does not work that way. As a simple illustration,
imagine a chess tournament, where, in a preliminary round, random
seating pits Gary Kasparov against Bobby Fischer, and Joe the Plumber
against my 5-year old Nephew. Kasporov and Joe win, making the first
round score: Kasparov 1, Joe 1, Fischer 0, Nephew 0. From this
score, it is obviously unreliable to conclude that Joe is as good a
player as Kasparov, and a better player than Fischer.

But the theory is that, given multiple preliminary rounds, the actual
best player at the tournament, even if he does not make #1, will at
least prove he is one of the top players, will at least end up with a
relatively high score. Hence, alot of players can be eliminated from
consideration.

The purpose of preliminary round scoring is not to choose the best, or
most deserving, player, but to eliminate from consideration a bunch of
people who are NOT the best or most deserving player. It is not
accurate enough for the former purpose, but it probably suffices for
the latter purpose.

One then takes the high-scoring players, and pits them against
eachother, on the theory that one of these people is probably the real
best player, and will now have an opportunity to prove it in a final
contest.

But if we handicap the contest in favor of the top-ranked player, we
are sabotaging the test, and begging the question.

Only if two players prove themselves equal in the final contest does
it make sense (for want of anything better) to use preliminary round
scorings as a tie breaker.

ranking (they cannot, for both the reason you illustrate above in the

involved and, like chess, the idea that the better player doesn't

round to give the person who performed the best in the preliminaries
(perhaps because of better demonstration of skill, perhaps by luck of
the draw in facing lesser opponents -- the rules seeding concept
doesn't distinguish between the two) the best spot (or xer choice of
spots if "best" isn't immediately obvious). Ski cross at the 2010
Vancouver Olympics, for example, lets the skiier with the best
performance so far (perhaps due to facing a weaker field in the
preliminary rounds) choose xer starting gate. Tennis seedings are used
to populate the elimination round in a way most favorable to the top-

comes time to set up the elimination rounds), but I may be wrong on
that point.

populate the finals (i.e., prelim performance, even though it could be
true, as your chess example above, that the #6 player is a better
player than #5 but simply faced a higher caliber of players during the
prelims than #5 did) can be used, and for the same reason, to provide
further ordering within the finals.

role of luck in the finals. (The reason, for example, that Short Track
switched from a random lane order in previous years for finalists to a

LSJ wrote:
> This is not "sabotaging" the finals, but rather helping to reduce the

To my mind, the appropriateness of the term "sabotaging" depends on
whether the measure reduces, rather than than increases, the
reliability of the test. This will depend upon whether the "reward"
is out of proportion to the achievement. The other sports-competition
examples you cite are not necessarily on point (almost certainly not),
because the proportion between the reward and the achievement may be
(and almost certainly is) very different.

In such competitions, the distinction between the first and second
seed may be far more meaningful. There may be many reasons for this.
Players may already have been sorted by skill (to a greater degree
than is possible in V:tES), before the preliminary rounds began.
Luck may be less of a factor in determining outcome of preliminary
rounds. Scoring may be different. Various multiplayer dynamics, far
beyond an individual player's control, may not apply.

On the other side of the equation, any advantage gained by the
privilege in such counter-examples may be extremely minimal. Does a
top-seeded racer really gain a substantial advantage from the
privilege of being able to choose his starting point? Probably not.
Probably the organizers have done their best to arrange the starting
points so that they are, to the best of their judgment, equal..

As for reducing the role of luck? Not really. Rather it increases
the role of a previous stroke of luck -- the stroke of luck that
resulted in a player being top seed rather than second or third seed.
And at least in V:tES (I cannot comment on those other games) this has
far more to do with luck than superior skill. And how about the
"luck" of overhearing someone say "so-and-so is playing his Arika
deck"? And how about the "luck" of knowing precisely what that means,
because you happen to come from that person's play-group.

Nor is "decreasing the role of luck" inconsistent with "sabotaging the
reliability of the test". It will also "decrease the roll of luck" if
we allow the top seeded player in an Axis & Allies tournament to play
with loaded dice. But this will also increase the chance that the
stroke of luck that made the player top seed will be more decisive
than it should be.

more likely measure than "random". That is, it will correctly
distinguish #1 from #2 (and #5 from #6) more often than random will.

Heaping slightly-meaningful syrup on the gravy is better than heaping
random syrup on the gravy.

> It is STILL less reasonable to give that top-seeded player a bonus
> whose value may range from virtually worthless, to almost decisive,
> depending on an out-of-game circumstances -- namely how much useful
> information he happens to have about his opponent's decks.

It is STILL less reasonable to leave that bonus up to random.

Using that out-of-game knowledge is not inherently wrong. It is
commonplace in other similar arrangements.

But, if there's an issue with scouting, then let that be the issue.

Isn't the issue really that if a top-seeded player has to choose
seating without knowing what some or all of the other decks do, then
they've lost the advantage they were supposed to have? VTES isn't
like a sport with easily accessible video recordings of other people's
matches or coaches who do the scouting for the players.

The stated goal of the final seating system is to give advantage to
finalists based on their ranking. The system is haphazard, since the
finalists need knowledge of the other finalists' deck in order to make
informed decision, thus gaining the advantage assumed by the system.
However, there is no mechanism in place to insure that they have a
chance to gain that knowledge.

Maybe we should talk about finding a formal way for players in a
tournament, or at least the finalists, to have the opportunity to gain
knowledge about all other players' decks.

Right.

> is better to use a merit system (if one can be found) to determine the

I don't agree with that either. (It might help, however, to define
certain phrases -- what is the definition of a "merit system"? Merit
is a loaded word, which implies that someone deserves something, which
further implies that he ought to receive it; which is to beg the
question being asked -- whether he should receive it or not).

Dice rolling matters in Axis & Allies. Do you agree with the premise
that, if dice rolling matters, it is better to use a merit system (if
one can be found) to determine battle results, than to do it
randomly? 'Cause I don't.

Same with V:tES. Like A&A, chance is a part of the game. Various
mechanisms are employed to achieve this. Decks are shuffled
randomly. But that is only the beginning. Added to this is an
elaborate "rock/scissors/paper" style randomness or Stratego style
randomness that results from the fact that you determine the contents
of your own decks, BUT NOT THE CONTENTS OF THE DECKS OF YOUR
OPPONENTS.

In V:tES, a wide array of factors, most of them beyond any individual
players control, collide to produce chaos. Skill matters, but a
skilled V:tES player is more like a skilled sailor riding a dangerous
and chaotic storm, than a God-like being moving pawns on a chess-
board. But that's what I like about the game, and I have no interest
in reducing the size of the waves, for the benefit of a particular
player.

Ideally, a player should not even know what decks he is facing. If he
does happen to have some knowledge of opposing decks, he should not be
able to further use this information by choosing which deck will be
his predator, or prey, or cross-table buddy.

> Random is random, yes. But the idea that it all averages out over many
> finals means that the seating order matters less is flawed. Each
> individual final's seating order matters just as much (to that final)
> whether it is done randomly or by some other means.

I'm not sure this is true. A player who receives an "advantageous"
position by chance may not know how to take advantage of the
advantage. However, a player who chooses an advantageous position
does so specifically because he believes he knows how to take
advantage of the situation.

> If the preliminary round performance is not a measure of merit, then
> it should not be used to determine final round seating (at best, it
> will simply be as good as random, and in practice it will be worse
> than random).

I don't acknowledge the connection drawn here. It is possible that
the tournament scoring system SHOULD give more weight to preliminary
round results. I have no reason to suppose that this is the case, but
supposing it were true, this only requires us to come up with a
tournament scoring system that gives more weight to the preliminary
rounds. It does not require us to handicap the final game in one
player's favor.

> > It is reasonable to guess that the best player at the tournament is
> > (probably) somewhere among the top five players, and therefore to hold
> > a game among these top 5 to determine which of these is truly best
> > (giving all players an equal chance at victory, and ignoring
> > preliminary standings except as needed for a tie-breaker).
>
> So it is a measure of merit.
>
> > It is FAR less reasonable to suppose that the preliminary standings,
> > as a measure of merit, are sufficiently precise to permit drawing a
> > meaningful conclusion that the top-seeded player has more merit than
> > the second-seed, etc. (Note that this factor already has potential to
> > be decisive even without the seating rule -- which might be okay, if
> > we did not try heaping syrup on top of gravy).
>
> It is sufficiently precise. Not because it is very precise, but
> because even a tiny bit of precision is sufficient. It doesn't have to
> be an absolute guarantee of perfect ordering, neither to be used to
> distinguish #6 from #5 nor to distinguish #2 from #1. It is simply a
> more likely measure than "random". That is, it will correctly
> distinguish #1 from #2 (and #5 from #6) more often than random will.
>
> Heaping slightly-meaningful syrup on the gravy is better than heaping
> random syrup on the gravy.

This argument proves far too much, as can easily be shown by carrying
it to its logical extreme. We can go much, much, further to eliminate
Randomness and the Unknown in favor of the top-seeded player, based on
the theory he is most "deserving" based on preliminary standings. We
can eliminate Chaos and replace it with Control. If we carry this far
enough, we effectively ensure his victory, and beg the question that
the final round is intended to test.

> > It is STILL less reasonable to give that top-seeded player a bonus
> > whose value may range from virtually worthless, to almost decisive,
> > depending on an out-of-game circumstances -- namely how much useful
> > information he happens to have about his opponent's decks.
>
> It is STILL less reasonable to leave that bonus up to random.

I disagree. I do not share this "Luck is bad and we have to get rid
of it" prejudice. I ask only that the game be fair, and Lady Luck be
given an equal chance to benefit all the participants. Let all
players expect the unknown and cope with the unknown. That is part of
the game. It is part of the challenge.

> Using that out-of-game knowledge is not inherently wrong.

Neither is going out for coffee between rounds. The caffeine-boost
may even help me win. That, however, would seem a poor excuse for
creating a rule specifically designed to reward coffee drinkers.

Except it the "merit system" has no "merit" unless used for
appropriate purposes. Using it to eliminate the bottom 15 players,
because probably none of them are "the best" is appropriate and
probably reasonably accurate. Using it to decide that #1 is more
deserving than #2 is entirely unjustified. The only excuse for

player, but to find the #1 player.

over the #6 player, is that we are looking for #1, and #5 is
significantly more likely than #6 to be a #1 player who got unlucky.

Sorry. I don't follow.

Not at all. How one scores the tournament is an entirely independent
question, and need not involve any alteration of the rules (or
customs) of the final game.

One could (for instance) add together the scores for the 4 rounds to
obtain a total score. Additional weight could be given to the final
game, by whatever factor one deems appropriate (x1.5, x2, x2.5, x3).
Make the factor sufficiently high (relative to the number of
preliminary rounds), and any Game Win in the final will assure victory
in the tournament as well. However, where no Game Win is scored in
the final, preliminary round standings would have more room to be
determinative than in the current system. Any number of variants of
this could be devised.

that the tie-breaker potential already gives preliminary rounds
adequate weight.

ordering of decks is sure to hurt someone at some point. Given the
choice of "handicapping" players decks at random, or via an already-in-
place-and-utilized measure of performance .... hey -- why NOT led the
leading player look through all everyone's decks and order them as he
sees fit?

Eventually it does, if you don't acknowledge a logical stopping
point. And it seems you don't because (if I understood you correctly)

reason not to pile syrup upon gravy (nor, presumably, more gravy upon

were eliminating randomness.

> The concept is merely to replace the replaceable chance elements in
> the finals with non-chance elements.

I know. But where is the stopping point? Because by the time you
finish with this process, you've given the whole game away.

This mis-states the issue. It is not a question of whether three
games are more reliable than one, but whether four games are more
reliable than three, and precisely how we use the fourth to further
refine the results of the first three.

We are not talking about using three games to separate the guy with 3
game wins from the guy with 0 game wins. That has already been done.
(And no-one denies that this distinction (1-1-1 versus 0-0-0) it is
more significant than than the difference between 1 game win and 1
game loss in a single round of preliminaries).

What we are talking about is distinctions among finalists. This
distinction usually amounts to no more, and often amounts to a good
deal less, than the outcome of a single preliminary game. Sometimes
distinctions even hinge on tournament points.

Even assuming that the difference between the top-seed and the second-
seed does amount to as much as a single game win, the game that they
are about to play (should someone win it) will be a far more
significant measure of the relative worth of these two players, for
all the reasons I first indicated. They are being measured directly
against each-other for the first time.

> One game is too small a sample size to determine which deck is
> "better".

Maybe, but the one game you play in the finals is still a better
measure than the one preliminary game (if even that) which separates
the finalists.

first or second after the preliminary rounds.

inevitably even these tend to vary in some significant way from their
classic archetype: more-stealth-less-combat, different kind of combat

at a critical moment. If you don't mind missing big chunks of a guy's
game, you can rely on such information. I don't think it's going to
help you that much, but go ahead. I still say the only information that's
really worthwhile is the stuff you gather at the table playing against
the guy.

Fred

preposterous work to try and prevent scouting, the game should simply
embrace it and assume that everyone is going to scout. And just not
worry about it.

Let people (assuming that they aren't otherwise disruptive) watch
games when they are done with theirs. Assume that they are going to
talk to people between rounds about what everyone else is playing.

information about the other finalists' decks is certainly helpful,

information you get from scouting is the information you get in 35
seconds when looking at a game in progress ("Huh. Bill has Ozmo and

information, and try to make sure that they can.

time out, and somehow get into the finals with zero time to walk
around and check out other games. But most of the time, not so much.

reasonably enforced as to be completely pointless. In game collusive
behavior is something that you can observe and make judgements about,
even if it is difficult to pick out sometimes. A couple of guys going
across the street to the pizza joint and comparing deck notes is not.

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
On Mar 22, 7:33 pm, "Frederick Scott" <nos...@no.spam.dot.com> wrote:
> The judge can only observe them if he's watching the game and paying
> close attention to who he thinks might be colluding.  How can he
> possibly do that if he didn't start out with a suspicion about them?
> In practice, I don't see the difference.

Other players can alert a judge to possible collusion in a given game--
if I think that Player A and Player B are acting incredibly wonky, and
it seems like they are working together for out of game reasons, I can
alert a judge. That isn't ever going to happen if people are secretly
sharing (illegal) information out of game (out of the room?).

In game collusion can be viewed and judged. Sharing secret (illegal)
information can't. That is the difference.

> I'm confused how anyone else would know (to point to something) either?

If two people are colluding in game, it is usually something that can
be pointed to/identified. Or is so subtle that it probably has no
effect.

-Peter
